https://www.politico.eu/article/andy-bur.text: LONDON — U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham engaged with messages from somebody impersonating one of Donald Trump’s closest advisers, four officials have told POLITICO. The new PM communicated with someone posing as White House chief of staff Susie Wiles before becoming suspicious that the contact was illegitimate, the officials said. “We do not comment on national security matters,” Downing Street said. One person briefed on the communications said a “few messages” were exchanged after the PM entered No. 10 but insisted they were “of no significance.” Advertisement Advertisement The British embassy in Washington was so concerned about the incident that it raised it with the White House, two of the officials said. Like others in this article they spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a matter of national security. Inside the U.K. government, there were fears that Wiles’ phone had been hacked again. The White House declined to comment. Last year, the White House and the FBI launched an investigation after senators, governors and U.S. business executives received texts and phone calls from someone claiming to be Trump’s chief of staff. The Wall Street Journal reported that Wiles told associates her cellphone contacts had been hacked . What was discussed in the exchange with Burnham — and when the messages were sent — is unclear, with the erroneous contact kept a closely-guarded secret. Burnham became PM on July 20, but it was clear he was on course to succeed Keir Starmer from the moment he won the Makerfield by-election on June 18. Advertisement Advertisement

Photograph: Vincent Yu/AP Hong Kong Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty in second national security case Wong, 29, is accused of urging foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades and other hostile measures against China Danny Vincent in Hong Kong Wed 2 Sep 2026 00.57 EDT First published on Wed 2 Sep 2026 00.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Joshua Wong , one of Hong Kong’s most prominent pro-democracy activists, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiring to seek foreign sanctions against Hong Kong and China, a national security charge that carries a maximum life sentence. Prosecutors have accused Wong, 29, of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China. The court heard that Wong had visited foreign countries and met foreign politicians to lobby for sanctions against Hong Kong and China. The prosecution said he had continued to call for sanctions on Hong Kong and China after the implementation of the national security law and that he had posted meetings on his social media accounts. Wong has been continuously imprisoned since November 2020. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027. ‘Hong Kong is at a crossroads’: inside prison with the student who took on Beijing Read more In 2022 he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. In November 2024 he was sentenced to four years and eight months in prison. Wong waved at supporters as he entered the dock. He wore a blue shirt and black-rimmed glasses. He stood with his arms behind his back as he pleaded guilty to the charges. Wong is expected to be sentenced later. The offence is punishable by a prison term of three to 10 years, or up to life imprisonment if the offence is deemed to be “of a grave nature”. Pleading guilty could typically result in a reduced sentence. Outside Hong Kong’s high court, people queued overnight to secure a seat at Wednesday’s hearing. One supporter who attended the court criticised the proceedings. “Under a compromised judicial system with zero space for a fair trial, Wong’s plea is a forced reality,” they said, asking not to be named. “This is not justice, but Beijing’s absolute eradication of Hong Kong’s dissident voices.” View image in fullscreen Hong Kong activist and supporters hold signs during a press event to support pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong in Taipei, Taiwan, on Wednesday. Photograph: Chiang Ying-ying/AP In 2014, the then teenage Wong became the international face of the Umbrella Movement, when thousands of protesters occupied major roads across Hong Kong for 79 days demanding greater democracy. In October 2014 he appeared on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”. When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the movement and immediately joined calls for the bill to be withdrawn. In 2020 Beijing imposed a wide-ranging national security law on Hong Kong after a year of anti-government protests. The authorities said the law was needed to restore stability to the international financial hub. Critics say six years on the law is continuing to expand in scope. Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law. Supporters say the prosecution heavily relied on his advocacy before the national security law was enacted and argue his case has been applied retroactively. “It’s obvious that the government wants to keep him behind bars for as long as they can, so as to isolate him and not to let him become a visible symbol of resistance.” said Frances Hui from the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation. Wong’s case has attracted widespread condemnation from global rights organisations. “By stacking one charge after another against Joshua Wong, the authorities are ensuring that the democracy icon stays behind bars, silencing him and the Hong Kong pro-democracy movement he helped lead and inspire,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Conflating promoting democracy and free speech with undermining national security is a favourite dodge for authoritarians. Beijing also likes blaming ‘hostile’, but unspecified foreign forces,” said Sophie Richardson, a longtime China rights advocate. On Tuesday the former Conservative leader Iain Duncan Smith urged the UK government to raise Wong’s case with Beijing, saying: “Enough is enough. It’s time to stop chasing peaceful protesters.” With Associated Press Explore more on these topics Hong Kong China Asia Pacific news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Amporn Sangkaew/EPA Thailand Australian man accused of murdering Thai teenager and putting body in suitcase pleads not guilty Simon Peter Carman appeared in a Pattaya court on Friday charged with killing Tunchanok Donhomla Agence France-Presse and Associated Press Fri 18 Sep 2026 06.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An Australian man accused of murdering a Thai teenager and putting her body in a suitcase pleaded not guilty on Friday in a hearing in the seaside resort city of Pattaya, a court official said. Simon Peter Carman, 45, was arrested in June after 17-year-old Tunchanok Donhomla was reported missing in Pattaya City, about 150km south-east of Bangkok. A suitcase containing her body was found shortly after. Police said she died of suffocation. In Thailand’s sex tourism hub, bright lights flash, loud music blares – and underage girls are exploited Read more Carman appeared on Friday at Pattaya provincial court, where he pleaded not guilty to all charges, a court spokesperson said. He had been charged with murder, concealing a body and taking a minor for indecent purposes. The next court date was set for 12 October. Police previously said CCTV footage showed him entering a condominium in Pattaya with the girl in the early hours of 25 June, and leaving that evening carrying a large black suitcase. In a police interrogation video shared online by Thai media, Carman has said he was acting in self-defence because the girl was threatening him with a knife. The case put the spotlight on Pattaya, which is popular with foreign tourists for its beaches and nightlife, but also has a reputation for sex tourism. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2d.text: Image source, Getty Images By Robert Greenall Published 18 September 2026, 14:00 BST Updated 24 minutes ago French President Emmanuel Macron has warned that the threat of hybrid attacks by Russia against Europe and France has intensified. In a news conference at the Elysee Palace, Macron said he had ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites in the face of this threat. He said France had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks which would not be left "without a response". A growing number of European leaders have warned that Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine. War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready? Published 16 hours ago Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary. These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary. The French president was speaking to journalists after meeting party leaders to discuss the security impact of the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. Macron mentioned last month's drone attack on Leipzig airport in Germany , blamed on Russia, and remarks by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggesting Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank. "In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified," he said. "The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine." On Thursday Tusk told Polish MPs that Russian plans included strikes by drones and missiles on countries supporting Ukraine. He said there was a "real risk" of such strikes on the territory of Nato countries, with Moscow then claiming that they were "accidental", in an attempt to split the alliance. Last Sunday, a Russian drone hit a passenger train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through along the same line. Ukraine said all the passengers had been evacuated just minutes before the strike at Yahodyn, which hit the train's engine. There have also been a number of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia . Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Russia does not plan to attack Europe, but Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned European nations against sending troops to Ukraine, which would be seen by Russia as a declaration of war. "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war, and it will be very short," he said. Meanwhile on Friday, Russia reiterated its warning to the UK that any British military facilities in Ukraine used to strike Russian territory were "legitimate targets". It reserved the right to take "necessary counter-measures" in response to the UK's "fiercely confrontational stance regarding Ukraine", referring to its supply of drones and other weapon systems to Kyiv. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Figure caption, Macron also addressed the energy situation, saying that the government had been tasked with protecting critical infrastructure and the "most sensitive" defence industry and technology sites against drone and cyberattacks. He also announced that France would call a meeting of the G7 to discuss energy and raise the question of gas stocks with the European Commission. "In the coming weeks, we will have a G7 meeting devoted to these energy issues, both to strengthen cooperation and to avoid unnecessary tensions between the G7 countries and our main partners," Macron said. "It will also be an opportunity to consider options for a possible release or unlocking of strategic reserves."
